description: Escaped the creepy weirdness of Bangkok for a calmer place here in Chiang Mai, in northern Thailand.  Got in pretty early but the heat wasn't motivating for touring around.  I went out at 7pm and it had cooled off by at least 10 degrees and few people were around.  This might be the plan (+ early mornings).  Then take refuge during the heat of day.  Had my first Khao Soi from its birth-region and it didn't disappoint.  I might write more about this dish later.  Not sure how long I'll be in CM - winging it at this point.

description: What a spectacular and challenging day.  I took a guided overnight tour that consisted of 3 parts.  A hike to a Karen Hill Tribe village in the mountains outside of Chiang Mai, an overnight stay and a return hike, then a visit to an elephant refuge and finally a float down this beautiful river on a bamboo raft.  That last one was super fun but no pics as I was worried about the phone.  This day was very challenging due to the combination of very significant heat and very steep climbs.  But we were rewarded with beautiful jungle scenery and rice paddies, an amazing waterfall, and finally the tribal village of the Karen people.  THey were very friendly and while very, very rustic the stay was a nice one.

Making our way towards the tribal village.  It was insanely hot in the sun and the amount of fluids that poured out of my skin was unbelievable
This saved the day as we cooled off here.  It was an amazing waterfall with a large cave behind it.  We had lunch at this beautiful spot

description: We were awakened at 5am by the roosters, dogs, chickens, pigs, and all sorts of activities.  Had a simple breakfast then it was 2 hours of hiking to another waterfall and our final destination.  It was another very hot day with extrememly steep climbs and descents.  The mosquitos were there but not too hectic.  Incredible scenery all around us.  We visited an elephant 'sanctuary' which really is just a money generating business where the elephants are paraded in front of you in close proximity.  Not my favorite sort of enterprise but it was a treat to see an Asian elephant up so close.  Then we went on a river float on bamboo rafts.  Very peaceful with some gentle rapids and a very nice finish to another arduous day.  Look for photo icons to the SW of Chiang Mai if you're interested in seeing where this trek was.

description: Not too many photos since this was a travel day.  About 4 hours in an utterly packed van filled with young folk and luggage.  It's a fairly dangerous 2-lane road to Pai, filled with huge trucks and blind turns and it rained during the 2nd half so it was a little but of a knuckle-biter.  Pai, as I'm discovering is very, very much a young person town.  And when people say it's a hippie place they really just mean it's a place for getting high.  O guess I should have realized but I just assumed that was like a part of it while I think it's really the main part of it.  So...  I still need to see what kinds of activities more my speed are available - that's my job tomorrow.  I may only be here 3 nights or so - we'll see.

And booked my pickup / border crossing / slow-boat ride to my first destination in Laos on Sunday.  It's a 2 day boat ride (I mean, they call it the slow boat) down the Mekong River with an overnight stay along the way.

description: It was a very long tour day with some really great stops.  Re-visited the White Temple which still just blows me away.  The artist who made this is just a genius.  There was a gallery of his stuff that was also incredible.  And the big bonus was a section I missed the first time called The Art Cave (or Art Garden - I think Cave...).  Just phenomenal.  This cave had so much detail with cool lighting, sculptures, music.  I found it hard to leave.  Then we hit the Blue Temple - another very cool, very modern temple not too dissimilar from the White Temple style.  Then the Black House or something like that which was an artist's (since passed) installation on this large property.  A lot of dark themes and unusual furniture and sculptures.  Another great installation.  Then to the tea farm which was pretty neato - Oolong tea tasting on a beautiful property.  Then the Tall Neck Village - which honestly was a little uncomfortable - but these people rely on this income as they are refugees from Myanmar.  You've surely seen at some point a documentary where the women of this tribe wear brass rings stacked on their necks that elongates them.  The older women still had these as did a few of the younger ones.  Felt weird taking pics so I didn't.  It was nice as there wasn't really a crowd and children were around playing their normal children games so the vibe was mostly fine.  Then the Golden Triangle which is the intersection of Thailand, Myanmar, and Laos.  Oh, and the Opium Museum which was sorta interesting - especially in that the area we spent most of the day in used to be predominantly occupied by opium fields.  Finally a quick stop at the Saturday Night Market in Chiang Rai, which I can still hear as I type this right before bed.  I have a very early morning tomorrow as I start my journey to Laos.  Should be an interesting one and it just might not be all that enjoyable.  Let's see how it goes!

description: A big travel day.  Went through Laos immigration and I have one weird story.  They want US$40 for the Visa.  I was warned they are very particular about the state of the bills themselves.  It turns out they are VERY, VERY particular.  Like no spots, crease marks, or defects of literally ANY kind.  I had 5 20's turned down and they finally took my 2nd $100 bill.  What a dump thing - they have some sort of money fetish here.  Also, $1 USD is equal to 21,340 Laotian "Kip".  Yeah.  I was told they take Thai Baht so I loaded up on that but I think that was a mistake because now I'm having to do 2 conversions just to know how much something is.  And they give you Kip for change anyhow so there's no avoiding it.  Sort of a mess but I'm sure I'll get around it.  Had a minor bad experience at the town we stopped - it's fully a we-got-you tourist trap and I some old guy hijacked my bag and insisted on payment for carrying it to shore afterwards.  Sux.  I suspect it's just this crappy town.  Hotel pretty rustic but at $13 per night what do you want?  So it's another long boat day tomorrow then hopefully things will be much better in Luang Prabang and I forked over for a pretty nice hotel there (like $35/night!!).

description: This was a much needed chill day.  Got my laundry in, got my tour for tomorrow sorted (full day), got my Vietnam E-Visa applied for, and had a little pool time.  Busy day tomorrow.

This is the most aggressive front grill I've ever seen on a vehicle before.  It sort of looks like the camera moved as I was taking it.  There are tons of Chinese cars in SE Asia and I suspect this is one of them.  Quite a few electric vehicles as well, 95% Chinese.  But I did see a few Tesla's in Thailand.  No Cybertrucks tho.

Sometimes you just need to have some tacos and Luang Prabang delivered.  They were quite good with the Lao beer and I had a great conversation with the owner (Lao) and her friend (former American from SoCal).  It's these moments that really recharge the solo traveler.  Group tours are great for that as well.  On all of my group tours I've had fantatic tour-mates.

A very long, full day.  Great crowd and had some good conversations which is nice to keep the spirits up.

I have my transport for tomorrow to  Nong Khiaw as well as my accomodations which will be much more rustic compared to where I am now.  Nong Khiaw is supposed to be a scenic village up north and is about a 3.5 hour drive from here.  Currently planning 3 nights there.  Sadly I have to double-back to Luang Prabang when I leave but then there's just a relatively short 50 minute train to my following destination of Vang Vieng - which used to be a 5 hour car ride.

description: It was about a 4 hour ride by mini-van to Nong Khiaw, a fairly small village alongside the Nam Ou river in Laos.  The journey was harrowing, with a small roaded loaded with massive trucks and craters that you almost couldn't see out of.  The abuse wrought by this road on the vehicles here is just wild.  But once I made it to Nong Khiaw, I had arrived at a truly beautiful place.  My room on the river is far, far nicer than I expected and the view is just incredible.  And for the cost of about $18/night.  It started raining just as I arrived and I walked through the actually very pleasant rain to a lunch spot where the extended family was taking shelter.  Had some nice grub then took a nap back at my room.  I don't have any specific plans for this place but I might very well extend my stay for a day or two, it's so nice here.  I hear rumors of hiking and boating options so might explore those.  No temples on the menu which is a nice change of pace.

description: A nice slow day in Nong Khiaw.  Really enjoyed the very cool morning and light rain.  It was maybe 68F out at most - the nicest morning of the trip so far.  Warmed up a bit in the afternoon but still pleasant.  Got an all-day tour set up for tomorrow and also got my multi-mode transport and itinerary settled for the next leg in a few days.  All of the places I'm visiting are very tourist-oriented (it's a lot of income for them - their main income in places like Nong Khiaw), so it's quite easy to book things and arrange transport.  I was thinking the transport out of NK might be double since "they got you".  You're in this relatively remote area so good luck getting out.  But turns out it was half the price of getting here.  No way to figure this stuff out.  Pricing is kind of all over the place.  LP's purely tourist stuff was the most expensive of all the cities I've been to so far - for no particular reason that I can figure out.  That said, the most I paid for an all-day tour out of LP was $94, which isn't all that bad.  The all-day NK tour was $34, so again, no idea how these number settle out.  These all-days include lunch, water, etc. and you're grouped so it's a good time to get some social interaction in.

description: Tour day.  We got in a mini-slow boat and travelled up river for maybe 45-60 minutes and then hiked up a very rough & steep trail to a viewpoint.  Then back down to a cave used as a shelter during the US bombing of Laos - some brutal history there.  Then to a village where we hiked to a waterfall.  I told this joke in the photo caption but it's just a good joke I'll tell it again:  I was considering another tour called the 100 waterfall tour (a long hike).  I think that's about 99 waterfalls too many so opted out of that one.  Haha.  Anyhow... we then boated downriver a bit and stopped and again had to shelter from a short rain storm.  Then we jumped into some kayaks (no pics for that one so as not to risk my phone) and paddled back go our starting point under the big bridge - fun!  Stubbed my little toe at the waterfall and it's black & blue but I should be alright.  Tomorrow will be another slow day then it's off to Vang Vieng the following day.

description: Not much to show for today.  It was a markedly much hotter day in Nong Khiaw.  Prior days have been relatively pleasant while today was downright hot.  Got a coffee/banana shake mid-day to fight the heat - yeah, that's a thing here.  Really good.  Let me describe my breakfast for you:  First of all, Asian Breakfast is not something I can abide.  Hot soup and noodle for breakie not good for me.  Bigger cities accomodate Westerners well.  These smaller towns do make an attempt but...  They offer these amazing sounding banana pancakes with those really sweet and crazy good local bananas.  But there is no such thing as maple syrup in SE Asia - certainly not in the smaller towns.  They offer honey but no can do - it doesn't work.  So I skipped that and got a breakfast sandwich.  See my comments on that pic for that part of the story.  The struggle is real.

photos.caption: As I was trying to figure out the pancake situation, I was trying to ask if they have bacon.  She had no idea and thought I was saying baguette.  I later looked up how to say bacon in Lao and wasn't too surprised by the result.  This was my predicament.  Gave up on the pancakes

description: Travel Day to Vang Vieng, Laos.  First I had to double-back on that thing they call a road.  The minivan was so crazy packed.  They often add locals to the ride and they get a special price.  There were not enough seats for everybody so some improvisation took place and some French passengers were not pleased and let the driver know it but what can you do at that point?  A key tip I caught onto very quickly (weeks ago):  GRAB THE FRONT PASSENGER SEAT!  Get that thing as quick as you can if you think it's going to fill up.  It's THE most comfortable seat in the vehicle and has the best view of the crater-filled road you will soon be lunar crusing on.  They squeezed in a tiny local older woman between me and the driver but she was small so I was perfectly comfortable.  And no, I didn't offer my seat - she was like half my size!  OK.  So then in Luang Prabang I had to get a tuk-tuk to the train station which was like 25 minutes outside of town.  Had some terrible food but it was air-conditioned so that was nice.  The train was actually very modern and very nice and it was a very quick ride to Vang Vieng.  Had to take another shuttle to the hotel as again the train station isn't right in town.  Staying at a fairly swanky hotel and got a room upgrade (go low season!).  The plan is 4 nights here then another train ride to Vientiane for a short stay then a flight to Hanoi.

photos.caption: Last morning Nong Khiaw
I'm going to miss this place - the most beautiful and my favorite of the trip so far
Hrmmm... the roads are no better going back to Luang Prabang
Nori Seaweed chips for the bumpy ride back to LP
The high speed train station in Luang Prabang.  I'm squinting because it was intensely bright at this moment
The single worst chili dog I've had in my life.  From the DQ at the train station.  I didn't have high hopes and boy did they deliver.
Inside the Luang Prabang high speed rail station, waiting for the train to Vang Vieng
Top speed is about 100 miles/hr.  It's a 50 minute ride.  The car ride would have been about 5-6 hours.  Probably half of the ride was in tunnels through the mountain area here.
I heard that ballooning is a thing here and immediatley saw this from my patio view.  I think I saw $65 for a 30min sunrise/sunset ride.  Maybe...
I got my western food fix at Gary's Irish Pub.  I was clued into this place by these 19 year old's on my last tour.  Many thanks to them I even got a Guinness on draft which is a real find
View in Vang Vieng, near the river and my hotel

Pool sunset view
More pool sunset view
MOAR ZOOM

description: Sadly, today was a sick day.  Started coming down with a sore throat yesterday afternoon.  Fever today so I was indoors most of the day.  Stepped out for some laundry service and food.  No plans for tomorrow as I'm going to see how I feel.  One thing about this place, is it's very hard to maintain being hygeienic around food.  You're constantly handling filthy money as most places don't take cards and there's not mucb in the way of soap around outside your hotel room.  And you'rr in typically pretty high population densities so like my last Thailand trip, it seemed inevitable to get me at some point.  That said, I'm not doing all that bad and hope I'll be back in business in a day or two.  Wouldn't say VV is my favorite place but it would be nice to get at least 1 or 2 activities in before I move off to the capital city of Laos, Vientiane.

photos.caption: It rained rather hard most of the morning and into early afternoon
Roti lady.  This time I got the savory roti with chicken, ham, egg, cheese.
The final roti - not bad - kind of a crunchy dough with filling

description: Felt like crap for most of the day so was almost entirely in my room.  Popped Advil on a 4-hour schedule.  Got my train ticket for the 28th.  Did a lot of TouchDesigner tutorial work on my laptop - maybe someday I'll have something to show from it.  It's quite complex so that may be awhile.  Sure hoping tomorrow I feel better.  No worries - not feeling that bad - just fever impacts.  Hoping tomorrow is a better day.  No Daily Thing today, sorry.

photos.caption: View from breakfast at my hotel this morning
Part of my breakfast - most of the nicer hotels here have a cook to make different egg dishes - I always go for the omette with everything

description: My bad - another sick day.  I think there are pretty fair odds I caught the Nimbus Coronavirus given the range of symptoms and severity.  Who knows, though?  Last night wasn't fun with tons of dreams/hallucinations that were just insane.  Fever broke and my sheets felt like it had rained inside the room.  By the way, last night there was one of those lightning strikes outside my window where there was virtually no delay between light and the giant F'ing boom!  So mostly felt like crap today.  I think I'm doing a little better this evening so I have hope for tomorrow which is a short travel day to Vientiane.

Front of my hotel next to the really rickety bridge across the river
Sunset on the river
Watch your step.  Also, there's a constant stream of scooters and motorcycles so watch them too.
Final sunset pic

description: Not a great night last night but generally feeling better throughout the day.  Train ride wasn't too bad.  Made it to Vientiane, the capitol city of Laos.  I was told by several people that it's a crap city not worth visiting and well... they were right.  I do have a full day tomorrow before my flight the next day - not sure what I'll do as my venture out tonight did not impress.  About that venture:  I had some really (relatively) expensive crap food at the rooftop restaurant.  Had a hankering for dessert but they no have dessert.  I figured, worst case I can find a market with a freezer and some ice cream.  It was dark by this point and I started down the busy, but small street of my hotel.   It was ultra sketch and just got sketchier the further I went.  Dark, quiet, industrial streets with me the only white guy in at least a few square miles.  But I was on a mission for some ice cream so I just put my head down and walked fast.  I found nothing on the roughly 2 mile walk I made.  But I did find success when I made it back to the hotel, looked across the street and spied a very tiny market that what-do-you-know had one of those ice cream freezers.  That Magnum bar was one of the better things I've had in awhile, let me tell you.  Food has not impressed lately though this is partly due to me illness and not wanting to venture very far.  Tomorrow's likely to me lame city but then I'm off to Vietname the next day where some real adventures should begin soon and I should be healthy to take them on again.

photos.caption: So now I know why Laos has a high speed rail system and just broken, crap roads.  China paid for most of the new rail system and it extended up to the Chinese border.
This white guy with the coolie hat:  what a baller

Dennis inception

description: Still not fully recovered but getting there I think.  Didn't do much of anything here - took some naps to help recover.  I did take a stroll of several miles in the incredibly cool (but humid) evening to visit the night market.  Like the city itself, it wasn't the most impressive night market.  Can you tell I'm ready to get out of here?

photos.caption: The Mekong is not quite as majestic here.  Man, I'm sorry to say it but this city is a hole.
Another night, another night market

description: Travel Day.  Nothing could be in such stark contrast as taking off from the Vientiane, Laos airport (it's the capitol city of Laos) and landing in Hanoi, Vietnam.  The airport of Hanoi looks similar to what you'd see in Seoul:  a very, very modern and large international airport.  The Vientiane airport was in rough, rough shape and had 5 very rough-looking gates.  I had not previously considered the third-worldness of Laos and the (seemingly) non-third-worldness of Vietnam.  Mind you, I've only really seen the airport and my view to my apartment was heavily clouded by very strong, windy rain.  But the city - what I've seen of it - is also in stark contrast with Vientiane.  I'm sure Hanoi was quite different only 20 years ago.  Anyhow, I've heard good things about Hanoi and am happy to be here.  It will be interesting to contrast Hanoi with some of the smaller villages I'm sure to visit over the course of this next 1-1.5 months.  I should add that I hate to say I still have lingering sick that is stuck on me.  Not bad - but still in a rather weakened condition that is going to make exploring & touring difficult until I can fully shake this thing.  I haven't been this taken down by sickness - well maybe ever.  I'll probably just start with some short, nearby explorations of the city.  Which sounds great to me.  Like some Vietnamese coffe shops, etc.  And really, I need to put my Vietnam plans into better shape, including Hanoi.  I think it would be interesting to see some "war stuff" but also I think this city has much more to offer as well.

photos.caption: The heavens unleashed shortly after I landed in Hanoi
This actually is a pic of a Pickleball shop for my brother Randy.  You'll just have to trust me on that one.
The alley outside the door to my unit.  Staying at a 'homestay'.  It's basically just a collection of very small apartments.

description: Got out for about 2 miles or so but then my body wore out and called it a day - yes, it sux.  But anyhow, I did a few things.  First, had some Vietnamese salt coffee (which I think is also known as egg coffee).  Both sound gross but it was quite good (some guy I met weeks ago had mentioned it to me).  Sort of a blended sweet egg frothy thing with the coffee (chilled).  Just not enough liquid - finished in about 3 gulps.  Went to the Temple of Literature which I read is more literally the Temple of Confuscious (there's a buddha-like statue of him there - people were praying to him which I found interesting).  Originally built in 1020 but rebuilt several times afterwards.  I had plans to proceed to 3 or 4 more destinations but got a little side-tracked when I looked to my left as I crossed a street and saw what appeared to be this famous alley-sized 'street' with a railroad running down the middle.  It's a tourist trap but sorta cool.  You can sit there and when the train comes by and the staff will pull the tables and chairs up and you can go "ooooh..., look at the train, it's so close".  I didn't do that myself - turns out the next train was like 4 hours later haha.  A funny piece to this story is I had been hearing this heavy rumbling intermittantly from my apartment.  Took awhile to realize it was a train - I'm in a very dense commercial area and hadn't seen any tracks so that was confusing.  It's loud but there aren't many runs so it didn't really bother me.  ANYHOW... this is the same train.  It's like right next to me.  The train.  At that point I was very thirsty and starting to feel tired so I decided to head back to my place a get some water and rest.  I took a long nap but never really recovered the mojo to get out there again.  I will head out in a bit for some food.  When I have a bigger appetite I will be trying Bun Cha which sounds incredible - look it up.  Some day my body will recover.  I just hope it's sooner than later.

description: Feeling quite a bit better today.  In fact, in 2 separate outings I walked a totatl of 7.1 miles!  That is a huge boost.  Still a few lingering things but on the whole much better!  Got 2 weeks of touring all sorted out this morning.  Headed over to Hoa Lo Prison, which was known as the "Hanoi Hilton" during the Vietnam War.  Did you know they call it the American War here?  This is also the prison that held Senator John McCain for 5-1/2 years.  I'm of course, in Vietnam so the focus of the tour/exhibits was the time that the Vietnamese revolutionaries were held here by the French and the atrocities they suffered.  The American part of the story was here but it seemed to be sorta shuffled off the main path in an upstairs area.  And the treatment of prisoners was pretty whitewashed.  Let's get real:  America's record on the treatment of "wartime" prisoners isn't so hot lately.  It was interesting to see, though only about a fifth of it is intact.  I didn't realize that Senator McCain was shot down just a few blocks from where I'm staying.  Did you know he broke both his arms and a leg in the process and he nearly died?  Go look up where he tells the whole story - it's quite interesting.  I moved on from there and basically just did some city walking, grabbed some lunch and headed back to my crib.  Not trying to overdo it as I step out of this illness.  One more full day in Hanoi tomorrow then it's off to the Ha Long Bay area for a cruise!

Most unfortunate

What's interesting about it is that it bears the marks of 2 cannon hits from the French in the late 1800's.  Oh, the French have very much to blame in the whole mess this country went through.
Side view of that gate

description: First of all, last night ended with a nice dinner provided by the host of the place I'm staying at.  Joined with a group of maybe 8 other travelers.  It's always nice to hear/share stories with co-travelers along the way.  Today:  This morning I headed over to the train street as it was only about 10 minutes away and crowds were light.  Bought a coffee as my entry fee, got a great spot and got some pics/video.  It was brief but kinda thrilling.  Headed over to the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum.  Normally his embalmed body is on public display but - and I don't know how accurate this is - the rumor has it that his body is on loan to Russia.  I dunno.  I missed seeing it - how many times do you get to see an embalmed body of a famous person?  Still, the grounds were pretty cool, very expansive, and very wet once the torrents unleashed.  Very heavy rain and lightning everywhere.  I enjoyed just hanging out and watching the lightning strikes all around me.  This site had the biggest crowds I've seen to date.  Had a very nice walk back and chilled for a bit.  Next mission: Bun Cha

description: This trip has been a real struggle at times.  Last night I developed some severe diarrhea and upset stomach.  In the morning vomiting.  Clear signs of food poisoning.  I suspect the Bun Cha but who knows.  So it was a very unpleasant day.  Started feeling worse in the afternoon and decided it was time to seek a clinic.  I was feeling so bad I just directed ChatGPT to find me a well-rated English-speaking clinic in the area.  Got a taxi there and it was a really nice, professional, modern clinic.  They took blood & stool and put me on some major fluids with an iv and also gave me anti-nausea drugs.  Was taking fluids for several hours.  They confirmed an infection and likely food-borne.  So got some antibiotics he thought were more appropriate and some anti-nausea meds.  I’ll be honest, once you have been so burned by your food it’s hard to remain confident as the impact is so harsh - as you know, it’s just such an intensely bad feeling when you get food poisoning.  So it’s hard to feel good about the next 1.5 months food-wise.  I dunno….  Fairly demotivated at the moment.  Was reading up on Vietnam and Hanoi in particular and they have had some recent isses with an increase in food poisonings.  Doesn't give me confidence for the next 2 months.

photos.caption: At the clinic getting fluids, anti-nausea, etc.

description: I'm in a seriously low internet cell coverage area so I can't in good conscious consume all of the bandwidth on this boat for pic uploads.  Going to attempt to upload 1 - if you see it I was successful.  I should be able to make a proper update tomorrow - hopefully.  I'm over my food sickness other than my present fear of Vietnamese food haha.  Going to leave it that.  I have some good pics of these past few days that I hope to post soon!

description: So I'm actually in Hanoi for a few hours as I await my overnight sleeper bus to the Ha Giang Loop area - not going to update my location until I get to Ha Giang.  After last night on the bay, we did a short bike ride and then caught our bus back to Hanoi.  Had a good time on Han La and Long Ha Bays.  Quite a few cruise ships about but met some nice people and we had fun.  I actually was with 2 groups due to most people doing the 1 night option while I did a 2 night stay.  Looking forward to the Ha Giang Loop which will be on the back of a motorcycle with a guide (in a group tour).  According to folks I've spoken with it should be one of the highlights of Vietnam.  Actually hoping for at least some rain as it's started to get quite hot lately with little breeze to cool things off.

description: Updated!  Got in late last night to Sapa after a 6 hour bus ride from Ha Giang.  The prior 4 days were a group motorcycle trip with 6 other riders.  We all elected (as do 99% of tourists) to do the "easy rider" option where we have a driver.  We had to pack light as there was so support vehicle.  It's all a little sketch but I only saw one very minor spill the entire trip (that is a crazy story:  this truck left behind a large trail of oil - yes OIL - on a steep mountain downgrade.  A good samaritan was out warning bikes and cars to stop due to oil on the road.  My driver took it very easy - another one not so much and he and his rider when down - unhurt.  Some very large trucks in front of us were sliding down, barely in control.  Anyhow - we made it down ok).  We'd stop frequently - every place had a coffee shop / refereshment stand.  The univerally agreement was that the coconut coffee was the best - it came in varying forms but is basically a sweet, iced coffee/coconut combo.  We'd retire at a homestay every night - do group meals and karaoke.  There was a tradition of drinking shots of "Happy Water" (very strong rice wine).  My group of 20-somethings were super fun and nice and the Aussie's put on the pressure for shot after shot so I had to not embarrass the USA so followed suit.  It was a lot of fun.  Anyhow, overall it was a series of rides, activities, eating, drinking, singing, and hanging out - a great tour with unbelievable views.
